rows.title: Climate resilience in planning refers to the ability
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Apply climate resilience and disaster-responsive planning principles to CLUPs and site planning, integrate hazard mapping and risk assessment into land use decisions, design for typhoon, earthquake, and flood resilience, and apply RA 10121 DRRM framework.

Climate resilience and disaster-responsive planning integrate hazard awareness into land use decisions, requiring planners to incorporate risk mapping, setback standards, and resilience frameworks into comprehensive land use plans. The Philippine context—exposure to typhoons, earthquakes, and flooding—makes this both a planning priority and a legal mandate.

## Core Concept

Climate resilience in planning refers to the ability of settlements and urban systems to withstand and recover from natural hazards and climate-related disturbances. Disaster-responsive planning goes beyond reactive recovery; it incorporates risk reduction into land use planning, infrastructure design, and community preparedness from the outset.

In the Philippines, disaster risk is not abstract—the World Bank estimates annual GDP loss to disasters at _1.9%_, driven by typhoons, floods, earthquakes, and storm surge. Legal frameworks, beginning with RA 10121 (Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2010), mandate that Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs) mainstream disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) into zoning and land allocation decisions.

Climate-resilient planning typically addresses:

1. **Hazard mapping and risk assessment** — identifying earthquake faults, flood zones, storm surge zones, landslide-prone slopes
2. **Setback requirements** — minimum distances from hazardous areas (active faults, water bodies, fault traces)
3. **Land use restrictions** — prohibiting residential or critical infrastructure in high-risk zones
4. **Building typology and resilience** — designing structures to withstand anticipated hazards
5. **Community resilience capacity** — ensuring access to evacuation routes, safe zones, early warning systemPost-Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan, 2013), some LGUs adopted 40-meter coastal buffers as local policy; national standards follow PD 1067 waterway easements.as, reflecting lessons from storm surge inundation. Active fault proximity is assessed per NSCP 2015 seismic design provisions and local ordinances; PHIVOLCS provides fault mapping for site-specific risk evaluation.e.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-008-01-core-concept" type="image" caption="Climate Resilience Planning — Hazard Mapping for CLUPs" description="Composite hazard map for CLUP integration: flood hazard zones (100-year floodplain), typhoon wind speed zones, earthquake fault buffers, landslide susceptibility zones, and sea-level rise projections. RA 10121 DRRM framework mainstreaming with adaptation measures." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers={["Legal Framework / Standard", "Key Requirement", "Application"]} rows={[["RA 10121 (DRRM Act, 2010)", "DRRM mainstreaming in CLUPs; 5% Local DRRM Fund per Sec. 21", "All LGUs must integrate DRRM into land use planning; funds support early warning systems, evacuation planning"], ["PHIVOLCS Active Fault Map", "5-meter minimum setback from fault trace", "Inhabited structures prohibited within 5m of mapped active fault; applies to all development"], ["Post-Yolanda National Zoning Framework (2014)", "40-meter no-build zone from mean high tide", "Coastal communities must maintain 40m buffer from high tide line; restricts new residential/commercial development"], ["CLUP integration (RA 7160)", "CLUP must incorporate DRRM; periodic review per DILG guidelines", "Planners must identify hazard zones on land use maps; review and update hazard mapping every 3 years"]]} />

## Philippine Context

The Philippines ranks among the world's most disaster-prone countries, facing an average of 20 typhoons annually, persistent earthquake risk along major fault systems, and increasing flood risk from sea-level rise and intense rainfall. The 2013 Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) storm surge inundated coastal cities and resulted in policy reforms, including the 40-meter no-build zone standard. Planners working in Philippine LGUs must balance development demand against mandatory hazard setbacks, making DRRM-informed CLUP revision a continuous practice.

## How It's Tested

1. **Hazard identification from site context** — "A proposed residential subdivision is mapped on a PHIVOLCS fault trace. What minimum setback must be maintained?" → Answer: 5 meters (from PHIVOLCS standard). Test assesses knowledge of numeric standards and source.

2. **CLUP integration and legal mandate** — "Under RA 10121, what must all LGUs mainstream into their CLUPs?" → Answer: Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM); this tests the legal requirement under Philippine planning law.

3. **Coastal hazard zone application** — "A municipality is planning a new fishing settlement 25 meters from mean high tide. Does this comply with post-Yolanda zoning standards?" → Answer: No, the standard requires 40 meters. This tests application of the numeric standard to planning scenarios.

<Tip>Memory aid: **PHIVOLCS = 5 meters** (both words start with one significant value: PHIVOLCS fault setback). **Post-Yolanda = 40 meters** (easy to recall as a protective buffer roughly the length of 10 houses or 1.5 city blocks).</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Climate adaptation = adjusting to actual/expected climate effects. Mitigation = reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Resilience = ability to withstand and recover. Know which strategies are adaptation vs. mitigation — the LEA tests this distinction.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-005-04** (DRRM) for site-level hazard integration, **LEA-PLAN-001-05** (CLUP Process) for resilience mainstreaming in CLUPs, and **LEA-PLAN-003-06** (Informal Settlements) for resettlement due to hazard exposure.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing the 40m coastal setback (post-Yolanda framework) with PD 1067 water body easements (3–40m depending on water body type). Remember: 40m no-build zone applies specifically to MEAN HIGH TIDE in coastal areas post-Yolanda; PD 1067 easements are broader water-body protection requirements.", "Stating that PHIVOLCS setbacks are 10 meters or 3 meters instead of 5 meters. The PHIVOLCS standard is specifically 5 meters minimum from active fault trace.", "Treating DRRM as optional in CLUPs. RA 10121 mandates DRRM mainstreaming; it is a legal requirement, not a best practice.", "Assuming all disaster-prone areas must be no-build zones. Setback standards allow development OUTSIDE the restricted zones; the zones restrict but do not eliminate development."]} />

rows.title: Planning in the Philippines
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

Philippine urban planning history is shaped by three distinct eras: Spanish colonial grid-plaza planning, American City Beautiful intervention, and postwar devolution to local authority. 
## Learning Goal

Trace the evolution of Philippine urban planning from the Laws of the Indies (1573) through the Burnham Plan of Manila (1905) to the Local Government Code (RA 7160, 1991), and identify the planning frameworks, key figures, and legacies of each period.

## Core Concept

Planning in the Philippines emerged from colonial intervention rather than indigenous settlement organization. The **Laws of the Indies (1573)**, Spain's urban planning code for colonial territories, mandated a strict grid-plaza town plan for all settlements — a central plaza surrounded by the church, municipal hall, and administrative buildings, with streets in a regular grid radiating outward. Every Philippine town established during the 300-year Spanish colonial period (1565–1898) followed this template, from Intramuros (Manila's walled core) to Vigan, Cebu, and provincial capitals. This colonial inheritance created the characteristic spatial organization of Philippine towns: centralized civic nucleus, regular street grid, and defined public plaza.

The American colonial period (1898–1946) introduced modern planning principles through **Daniel Hudson Burnham's Plan of Manila and Baguio (1905)**. Burnham, the architect of the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition and the City Beautiful Movement, was commissioned by the American colonial government to create a grand planning vision for the Philippine capital and the new Highland Summer capital. The **Plan of Manila (1905)** proposed sweeping reforms:

- Luneta (now Rizal Park) as the grand civic focal point, expanded with landscaping and monuments
- Taft Avenue as the main ceremonial boulevard, connecting downtown to the bay
- Regularization of the Pasig River with tree-lined embankments and public walkways
- Intramuros fortification preservation as a historic core, with new government buildings and civic spaces
- Park system development to civilize the tropical city
- Infrastructure modernization (sewage, water, streets) following City Beautiful principles

The Plan of Manila was only partially implemented — wartime destruction, budget constraints, and changing political priorities meant many Burnham visions never materialized. However, Luneta, Taft Avenue, the Pasig River embankment, and government building placement in Manila reflect Burnham's legacy. The Plan of Baguio (also 1905) was more successful; the grid street layout, Wright Park, and overall urban form of Baguio closely follow Burnham's design.

Post-independence planning (1946–1970s) focused on national reconstruction and city expansion, but lacked comprehensive frameworks. The **Local Government Code (RA 7160, 1991)** marked the watershed moment, devolving planning authority to all municipalities and cities and mandating **Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs)**. This shift acknowledged that centralized planning had failed to manage rapid urbanization, informal settlements, and environmental degradation. Contemporary Philippine planning now operates through LGU CLUPs reviewed by **DHSUD** (formerly HLURB), integrated with housing policy (RA 7279), environmental protection (PD 1586, PD 1067), and disaster risk reduction (RA 10121).
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-001-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Philippine Urban Planning History — Spanish, American, and Post-War Eras" description="Timeline diagram showing three eras: (1) Spanish colonial grid-plaza system (Law of the Indies), (2) American City Beautiful — Burnham's Plan of Manila 1905 with diagonal boulevards and civic core, (3) Post-war devolution under RA 7160 (1991 LGC) with CLUP mandate." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers=["Historical Period", "Planning Framework", "Key Figure(s)", "Legacy"] rows=[["**Spanish Colonial (1565\u20131898)**", "Laws of the Indies (1573) \u2014 grid-plaza mandated for all towns", "Spanish Crown; local governors", "Every Philippine town follows grid-plaza model; Intramuros as walled core"], ["**American Colonial (1898\u20131946)**", "Burnham Plan of Manila (1905); City Beautiful Movement", "Daniel Hudson Burnham", "Luneta, Taft Avenue, Pasig River development; Baguio city plan"], ["**Early Independence (1946\u20131970s)**", "Ad hoc urban expansion; minimal comprehensive planning", "Various \u2014 fragmented authority", "Rapid unplanned growth; informal settlements proliferate"], ["**Devolution Era (1991\u2013present)**", "Local Government Code (RA 7160) \u2014 CLUP mandate for all LGUs", "National and local government", "Planning authority decentralized; CLUPs as strategic tool; DHSUD oversight"]] />

<WikiExamTable headers=["Concept", "Significance", "Testable Detail"] rows=[["**Laws of the Indies (1573)**", "Spanish colonial urban planning law; mandated grid-plaza pattern for all NEW colonial settlements", "Every Philippine colonial town follows this template \u2014 not a tax law or military order"], ["**Burnham Plan of Manila (1905)**", "Comprehensive master plan for Manila and Baguio; City Beautiful Movement applied to tropics", "Luneta expansion, Taft Avenue as ceremonial boulevard, Pasig River embankment development, government building placement"], ["**City Beautiful Movement**", "Aesthetic urbanism: monumental civic spaces, diagonal boulevards, parks, grand design", "Applied in Manila; contrast with later functionalist/pragmatic approaches"], ["**Luneta (Rizal Park)**", "Manila's grand civic space; Burnham Plan centerpiece", "Focal point of City Beautiful design; symbol of colonial and national governance"]] />

## Philippine Context

Contemporary planning in the Philippines is structured by **RA 7160** (Local Government Code, 1991), which ended centralized planning and created a system where every municipality and city prepares a 10-year CLUP. This represented a philosophical shift: recognition that top-down national planning had failed to address squatter settlements, traffic congestion, and environmental degradation in Manila and other cities. The CLUP system decentralizes authority while maintaining national standards through **DHSUD** review.

The historical tension between centralized City Beautiful aesthetics (Burnham's Manila) and practical equity concerns (housing for the poor, upgrading informal settlements) continues to define Philippine planning debate. Modern planning integrates both: aspirational citymaking (BGC, urban renewal districts) and social housing (RA 7279 balanced housing requirements, NHA resettlement projects). Understanding planning history helps explain why contemporary debates emphasize _both_ livability and equity — colonial and American legacy provides the design vocabulary; postcolonial nation-building demands inclusion.

## How It's Tested

The LEA tests Philippine planning history through two dominant question patterns: (1) **Historical attribution and detail** — "The Laws of the Indies were Spain's urban planning law mandating which town pattern?" (Answer: grid-plaza). "The Burnham Plan of Manila (1905) proposed which of the following?" (multiple improvements listed). "Which feature of contemporary Manila reflects Burnham's legacy?" (Answer: Luneta, Taft Avenue, or Pasig embankment). (2) **Postcolonial institutional history** — "RA 7160 marked a shift from centralized to decentralized planning. What was the new planning instrument mandated for all LGUs?" (Answer: CLUP). Questions rarely ask for philosophizing; they test factual knowledge of dates, theorists, and specific projects.

<Tip>
**Historical memory anchors:** LAWS OF THE INDIES = 1573, Spanish planning law. Every Philippine town = grid-plaza. BURNHAM = 1905, Plan of Manila. Three Burnham legacies = LUNETA, TAFT AVENUE, PASIG RIVER. RA 7160 = 1991, devolution, CLUP mandate. DHSUD = 2019 creation (RA 11201) consolidating HLURB, NHA, and other housing/planning agencies.
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Three key dates: 1573 (Laws of the Indies), 1905 (Burnham Plan), 1991 (RA 7160 / Local Government Code). Know the exact year for each — 1988 or 1992 are NOT acceptable substitutes for RA 7160.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-001-01** (Planning Fundamentals) for theorist attribution, **LEA-PLAN-007-06** (Key Figures) for Burnham biography, and **LEA-PLAN-001-05** (CLUP Process) for post-1991 devolved planning system.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing the Burnham Plan of Manila with other planners — Burnham designed both Manila and Baguio (1905); do not attribute Baguio to other architects", "Thinking Laws of the Indies were tax or military laws — they were URBAN PLANNING laws mandating grid-plaza towns", "Forgetting that the Spanish colonial grid-plaza is the MODEL for all Philippine towns — students sometimes think Intramuros is unique", "Misremembering Burnham Plan date — it's 1905, not 1900 or 1910", "Attributing Luneta or Taft Avenue to contemporary planners instead of Burnham legacy"]} />

rows.title: Truss is a structural system of straight members
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Identify truss member types: top chord, bottom chord, verticals, and diagonals
- Distinguish Warren, Pratt, and Howe trusses by their diagonal patterns
- Apply the two zero-force member rules to identify unloaded members
- Explain why triangular geometry makes trusses structurally efficient

Trusses are skeletal structures composed of members arranged in triangular patterns to span long distances with minimal self-weight. Understanding truss member names, types, and the zero-force member concept is essential for structural analysis and LEA success.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-002-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Truss Types — Warren, Pratt, and Howe Comparison" description="Three-panel diagram comparing: (1) Warren truss — equilateral triangles, diagonals alternate in tension/compression; (2) Pratt truss — diagonals slope downward toward center (tension), verticals in compression; (3) Howe truss — diagonals slope upward toward center (compression), verticals in tension. Each panel shows member force labels (T/C), typical span range, and common application. Zero-force member identification rules illustrated." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

A **truss** is a structural system of straight members connected at joints (usually pinned connections) that form triangles. Trusses are efficient because triangles cannot change shape without changing member lengths, providing inherent rigidity and allowing members to carry primarily axial loads (tension or compression) rather than bending moments.

**Basic Truss Members:**

- **Top Chord**: The upper horizontal (or sloped) members forming the upper boundary of the truss.
- **Bottom Chord**: The lower horizontal (or sloped) members forming the lower boundary.
- **Verticals (or Vertical Members)**: Members oriented perpendicular (or nearly so) to the chords, connecting top and bottom chords.
- **Diagonals**: Members oriented at angles between the chords, typically in tension or compression depending on load direction and truss type.

**Truss Types by Geometry:**
- **Simple Truss**: Single triangular units, economical for short spans.
- **Warren Truss**: Diagonal members form a zigzag W pattern; efficient for distributed loads.
- **Pratt Truss**: Vertical members are in compression (short, efficient); diagonals slope inward from bottom, in tension (long, able to handle tension).
- **Howe Truss**: Diagonals slope outward; verticals carry tension (opposite of Pratt).

**The Zero-Force Member:**

A **zero-force member** is a member that carries no load (zero axial force) under a given loading condition. Zero-force members are identified using equilibrium equations at joints. They commonly occur when:
1. Only two members meet at a joint with no external load, and the members are not collinear—one member must have zero force.
2. Three members meet at a joint, two are collinear, and no external load acts at the joint—the third member has zero force.

Identifying zero-force members is critical for analysis simplification and for recognizing that some members may not be needed under certain load cases, although they may be needed under others.

## Key Provisions

| Truss Type | Chord Configuration | Typical Diagonal Pattern | Efficiency | Span Range |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| **Simple Truss** | Parallel or triangular | Single triangle | Basic, economical | Short (< 10 m) |
| **Warren** | Parallel | Zigzag W pattern | Good load distribution | Medium (10–20 m) |
| **Pratt** | Parallel | Diagonals slope inward from bottom | Good under gravity loads | Medium–Long (15–40+ m) |
| **Howe** | Parallel | Diagonals slope outward | Adequate; less common than Pratt | Medium (15–25 m) |
| **Pitched (Roof)** | Sloped top, horizontal bottom | Varies (Pratt, Warren) | Efficient for roofs | Medium–Long |

**Zero-Force Member Rules:**
- If two members meet at a joint with no external load and are not collinear, one is zero-force.
- If three members meet at a joint, two are collinear, and no load acts, the third is zero-force.
- Zero-force members can still be designed and included for redundancy or other load cases.

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, roof trusses (Warren or Pratt types) are common in agricultural buildings, markets, and industrial structures. Long-span trusses are used in gymnasiums, warehouses, and bridge structures. Steel trusses are preferred for their strength-to-weight ratio and durability in tropical climates. Timber trusses are used in residential and light commercial roofs.

## How It's Tested

**Remember-level:** Name the members (chord, vertical, diagonal) and identify truss type (Pratt, Warren, Howe, simple).

**Understand-level:** Explain why triangular geometry makes trusses efficient and why members carry primarily axial loads.

**Apply-level:** Given a truss with specific loading, identify zero-force members using equilibrium equations.

<Tip>**Memory aid:** "Chord connects, verticals connect, diagonals brace." Pratt has "inward diagonals" (think Pratt ≈ inward pointing). Zero-force: **two collinear, third bye-bye**; **two non-collinear, one zero**.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Space Frames** (lea-strc-002-06) for the 3D extension of trusses, **Supports** (lea-strc-001-03) for how truss end conditions affect analysis, and **Internal Forces** (lea-strc-001-05) for how truss members carry axial loads.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing chord (boundary member) with diagonal members—chords form the truss outline","Assuming all members are necessary in all load cases; zero-force members are valid and should be recognized but may not always carry load","Misidentifying Pratt vs Howe—Pratt: diagonals slope inward from bottom (compression); Howe: outward (tension in diagonals)"]} />

rows.title: Contemporary urban models
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Distinguish contemporary urban models — Garden City (30,000-60,000 pop), New Urbanism (400m walk radius), Transit-Oriented Development, 15-Minute City, CIAM — by their target values, design principles, and urban vision, and apply to Philippine urban scenarios.

Contemporary urban models—Garden City, New Urbanism, Transit-Oriented Development, and 15-Minute City—represent a reaction against sprawl and car-dependent development. Each model specifies exact distances, target populations, or design principles. The LEA tests precise values: Garden City = 30,000–60,000, not 100,000; New Urbanism walk radius = 400m, not 800m; CIAM = separation of functions, not mixing.

## Core Concept

Contemporary urban models are 20th and 21st century responses to the social and environmental failures of 20th-century modernism. They redefine what livable, sustainable cities should look like.

The **Garden City** (**Ebenezer Howard, 1898**) was conceived as a self-sufficient new town of _30,000–60,000 people_, large enough to support diverse employment and services but small enough to preserve community and greenspace. Howard envisioned combining the best of city (culture, employment, services) and countryside (fresh air, green space, agricultural buffer). Planned garden cities like Letchworth (1903, England) and Welwyn Garden City (1920, England) were built as standalone communities with clear boundaries, internal transit, and community land ownership. The Garden City concept influenced suburban development globally and partly inspired Quezon City's garden suburb aspirations.

**New Urbanism** (**Andrés Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, Peter Calthorpe, 1980s–present**) emerged as a critique of car-dependent sprawl. New Urbanism advocates for a return to traditional neighborhood design: walkable blocks, mixed-use neighborhoods, diverse housing types, and strong transit connections. The signature principle is the **5-minute walk**: all daily needs (groceries, services, parks, transit) within _400 meters_ of residential locations. This distance assumes a pedestrian walking speed of ~4–5 km/h. New Urbanism influenced mixed-use developments like Bonifacio Global City and infill projects near MRT stations.

**Transit-Oriented Development** (TOD) extends New Urbanism by anchoring development density around mass transit stations. The ideal TOD catchment is _400–800 meters from a station_—the upper bound represents a 10-minute walk. TOD zones typically allow higher density mixed use, parking reduction, and pedestrian priority. The wider catchment (vs. New Urbanism's 400m) accommodates secondary uses and residential options beyond the immediate walk zone.

**15-Minute City** (**Carlos Moreno, 2020**) is a contemporary refinement proposing that residents should access all daily needs—work, food, health, education, culture, parks—within _15 minutes by foot or bike_. Moreno developed this concept in Paris and it has influenced planning in European cities, Tokyo, and emerging urban frameworks globally. It extends beyond the 5-minute neighborhood to create a more functional daily-life radius while still prioritizing active transport.

**CIAM and the Athens Charter** (1933) represent the modernist precursor to contemporary urbanism—but with opposite values. CIAM (_Congrès Internationaux d'Architecture Moderne_) advocated dividing cities into four separate functional zones: living, working, recreation, and transportation. This zoning doctrine caused decades of urban dysfunction (dead downtowns, isolated neighborhoods, car dependency). Contemporary models like New Urbanism are explicitly a reaction _against_ CIAM's separation—New Urbanism advocates _mixed use_, blending residential, retail, services, and offices.

**Smart Growth** (1990s–present) is a set of principles emphasizing compact, infill development; walkability; transit; mixed uses; and environmental protection. Smart Growth rejects sprawl and car-dependent patterns. It is applied planning strategy rather than a single theorist's framework.

**Growth Pole Theory** (**François Perroux, 1955**) proposes that concentrated investment in a strategic economic sector or location generates "spread effects" to surrounding regions—agglomeration benefits that stimulate broader development. The Clark development corridor (New Clark City in Pampanga) and infrastructure investment corridors reflect growth pole thinking.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-002-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Contemporary Urban Models — Garden City, TOD, New Urbanism, 15-Minute City" description="Comparison diagram of modern urban models: Garden City (30,000-60,000 pop, greenbelt), TOD (400m transit radius, density gradient), New Urbanism (5-minute walk, mixed-use), 15-Minute City (all amenities within 15 min walk/cycle), and CIAM (functional zoning tower-in-park)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers={["Model/Approach","Theorist(s)","Year","Target Sclea or Radius","Key Principle"]} rows={[{"Model/Approach":"Garden City","Theorist(s)":"Ebenezer Howard","Year":"1898","Target Sclea or Radius":"30,000–60,000 people","Key Principle":"Self-sufficient new town combining city services with countryside amenities; community land ownership"},{"Model/Approach":"New Urbanism","Theorist(s)":"Duany, Plater-Zyberk, Calthorpe","Year":"1980s–present","Target Sclea or Radius":"400m (5-min walk)","Key Principle":"Walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods; all daily needs within walking distance; pedestrian-first design"},{"Model/Approach":"TOD","Theorist(s)":"Calthorpe et al.","Year":"1990s–present","Target Sclea or Radius":"400–800m from station","Key Principle":"Higher density, mixed-use development anchored to transit stations; reduced parking; active transport priority"},{"Model/Approach":"15-Minute City","Theorist(s)":"Carlos Moreno","Year":"2020","Target Sclea or Radius":"15 min walk/bike","Key Principle":"All daily needs (work, food, health, education, culture, parks) within 15-minute active transport radius"},{"Model/Approach":"CIAM / Athens Charter","Theorist(s)":"Le Corbusier, CIAM","Year":"1933","Target Sclea or Radius":"City-wide zoning","Key Principle":"Separation of four functions (living, working, recreation, transport) into distinct zones — OPPOSITE of mixed use"},{"Model/Approach":"Smart Growth","Theorist(s)":"Multiple practitioners","Year":"1990s–present","Target Sclea or Radius":"Urban-wide policy","Key Principle":"Compact infill, walkability, transit, mixed use, environmental conservation; anti-sprawl"}]} />

## Philippine Context

The Philippines adopted New Urbanism principles in Bonifacio Global City (mixed-use, walkable), proposed TOD frameworks around MRT extensions, and referenced 15-Minute City concepts in recent urban development guidelines. However, widespread car dependency, informal settlements, and fragmented land tenure make implementation challenging. Understanding contemporary models helps planners and architects advocate for walkability and mixed use in Philippine development while confronting structural barriers (transport network gaps, informal land occupation, limited affordable housing supply).

## How It's Tested

1. **Numeric values:** "New Urbanism's 5-minute walk radius equals how many meters?" Direct recall of 400m, not 800m (which is TOD).

2. **Theorist attribution:** "The Garden City concept of 30,000–60,000 people is attributed to whom?" → Howard (1898).

3. **CIAM vs. contemporary:** "CIAM's Athens Charter advocated for [separation / mixing] of urban functions." → Separation (CIAM advocated zoning; contemporary models oppose it).

4. **Application:** "Which contemporary model would best guide development around a new MRT station?" → TOD.

<Tip>**Memory anchors:** HOWARD = **30,000–60,000** (Garden City population). New Urbanism = **400m walk** (NOT 800m; that is TOD's upper bound). CIAM = **SEPARATION** (the problem that contemporary models react against). MORENO = **15 MINUTES** (all daily needs within active-transport distance).</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Know precise values: Garden City = 30,000-60,000 population (NOT 100,000). New Urbanism walk radius = 400m (NOT 800m). TOD = 400-800m transit radius. CIAM = separation of functions. 15-Minute City = all services within 15 min walk.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-002-01** (Classical Urban Models) for foundational models, **LEA-PLAN-008-03** (Sustainable Urban Development) for TOD and compact city principles, and **LEA-PLAN-002-06** (Urban Design) for New Urbanism design standards.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing New Urbanism's 5-minute walk radius (400m) with TOD's catchment (400–800m)—the upper TOD bound is double the New Urbanism standard","Stating Garden City target population as 100,000 instead of 30,000–60,000—students often round up to memorable large numbers","Thinking CIAM advocated mixed use—CIAM advocated SEPARATION of functions; mixed use is a contemporary critique of CIAM's legacy","Attributing Garden City to Howard but not stating the correct target population range—Howard's vision is specific about sclea for a reason"]} />

rows.title: Smart city uses interconnected digital systems
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Apply smart city concepts — GIS, IoT sensors, real-time data, digital platforms — to urban planning and city management, evaluate digital planning tools for Philippine LGUs, and identify opportunities and risks of smart city implementation.

Smart cities integrate digital technologies—GIS, real-time data, IoT sensors, and digital platforms—into urban planning and city management to improve efficiency, livability, and sustainability. Digital planning enables planners to visualize land use patterns, monitor infrastructure performance, and engage communities through data-informed decision-making.

## Core Concept

A smart city uses interconnected digital systems to optimize urban services, reduce resource consumption, and improve quality of life. Smart city planning moves beyond static paper maps to dynamic, data-driven systems that track transportation flows, energy use, water consumption, and air quality in real time. This capability allows planners and municipal managers to respond to problems (congestion, pollution, service failures) quickly and to anticipate future demand.

Digital planning tools include:

1. **Geographic Information Systems (GIS)** — spatial data management, layer analysis, overlays for constraint mapping
2. **Real-time monitoring and IoT sensors** — traffic sensors, air quality monitors, water meter data
3. **Predictive modeling** — traffic simulation, flood modeling, utility demand forecasting
4. **Digital civic engagement platforms** — online surveys, participatory budgeting, crowdsourced feedback
5. **Data visualization dashboards** — real-time displays of city performance metrics

Smart cities typically target sustainability goals—reducing carbon emissions, improving transit efficiency, minimizing waste—while enhancing livability through responsive services. A smart city does not replace traditional planning; rather, it extends planning's reach by providing real-time feedback on plan implementation and infrastructure performance.

In Philippine cities, smart city initiatives are emerging in high-growth urban centers where congestion, pollution, and resource strain demand efficient management. Digital planning supports the CLUP by making land use data accessible and enabling rapid updates when conditions change.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-008-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Smart City Planning Framework — GIS, IoT, and Digital Platforms" description="Diagram of smart city components: GIS-based spatial planning, IoT sensor networks (traffic, air quality, waste), real-time data dashboards, digital service platforms, and implementation considerations for Philippine LGUs. Opportunities and risks of smart city deployment." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers={["Digital Tool / Framework", "Primary Function in Planning", "Application Example"]} rows={[["GIS (Geographic Information Systems)", "Layer mapping of land use, hazards, infrastructure, constraints; constraint analysis", "Overlay flood zones, slope hazard maps, utility networks to identify viable development sites"], ["Real-time traffic monitoring", "Identify congestion patterns; assess transportation network capacity", "Detect peak-hour bottlenecks; prioritize transit corridor improvements; evaluate new development's traffic impact"], ["Air quality and environmental sensors", "Monitor pollution levels; identify environmental hotspots", "Data-driven decisions to restrict heavy industry proximity to residential areas; track air quality compliance"], ["Utility consumption dashboards", "Track water, electricity, waste generation in real time", "Identify water-loss zones in distribution networks; redirect development away from undersized utility zones"], ["Digital civic engagement platforms", "Collect community input on planning priorities; increase transparency", "Online CLUP surveys; participatory budgeting for neighborhood improvements; crowdsourced issue reporting"]]} />

## Philippine Context

Philippine cities face rapid urbanization—Metro Manila, Cebu, Davao, and secondary cities are growing faster than infrastructure can expand. Congestion, flooding, power shortages, and water scarcity are endemic in many urban areas. Smart city planning addresses these constraints by optimizing existing infrastructure before adding capacity. The national government and progressive LGUs (notably in Metro Manila and Visayas) are adopting GIS-based planning and real-time monitoring platforms. Digital engagement also supports the participatory planning mandate under RA 7160 (Local Government Code) and RA 10587 (Environmental Planning Act), making CLUPs and planning data publicly accessible online rather than locked in planning offices.

## How It's Tested

1. **GIS tool application** — "A municipality uses GIS to layer land use zones, flood risk maps, and utility capacity zones. What planning question can this overlay answer?" → Answer: Identifying suitable sites for new development that comply with zoning, avoid hazards, and have adequate utility support. Tests understanding of spatial analysis.

2. **Real-time monitoring and response** — "A smart city dashboard shows that a new commercial district is generating 40% more traffic than the CLUP's traffic impact assessment predicted. What does this inform the planner to do?" → Answer: Reassess the district's road network capacity; consider congestion mitigation (signal timing, transit alternatives, use restrictions); update traffic modeling in future CLUPs. Tests decision-making based on real-time feedback.

3. **Digital engagement and participatory planning** — "A municipality launches an online platform for residents to report potholes, blocked drains, and inadequate street lighting. How does this serve planning?" → Answer: Provides ground-truth data on infrastructure maintenance gaps; identifies priority repair zones; informs capital improvement plans. Tests the link between digital engagement and planning implementation.

<Tip>Memory aid: **GIS = Geographic Information Systems = spatial layer analysis**. Think of GIS as the digital equivleant of drawing transparent maps on overlays and stacking them to find patterns. **IoT = Internet of Things = real-time sensors feeding live data**. Smart cities collect constant data; static data is yesterday's planning.</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Smart city components: GIS (mapping analysis), IoT (sensors for traffic/air quality/waste), big data analytics (demand forecasting), digital platforms (e-governance, community engagement). Focus on PLANNING applications, not technology details.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-008-01** (Climate Resilience) for smart climate monitoring, **LEA-PLAN-002-06** (Urban Design) for smart streets design, and **LEA-PLAN-007-05** (LGU Planning) for LGU digital planning capacity.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing smart cities with just technology installation. Smart cities are not defined by having lots of sensors; they are defined by using integrated data to make better planning and operational decisions. A city with sensors but no data analysis is not a smart city.", "Assuming smart city planning replaces traditional CLUP processes. Digital tools support CLUPs; they do not eliminate the need for comprehensive land use strategy, public participation, and zoning ordinances.", "Overstating the autonomy of smart systems. Real-time data and AI models inform planner decisions; humans still decide policy. Smart cities are tools for human-centered planning, not robotic city management.", "Treating digital equity as irrelevant. Smart city benefits depend on equitable access to digital engagement platforms and services. Digital-only engagement excludes low-income and elderly populations; effective smart cities use hybrid analog-digital engagement."]} />

rows.title: Percentage-of-PCC method multiplies Project
rows.content:
## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Describe the fee structures for specialized architectural services.
- Explain how specialized services (interior design, urban planning) are compensated.
- Identify the SPP documents that govern specialized service fees.
- Distinguish specialized service fees from basic service fees.

Fee computation converts a project's estimated construction cost into architect compensation using classification-specific percentages established in the Architect's Guidelines and SPP documents. This calculation is foundational to professional practice and frequently tested.

## Core Concept

The percentage-of-PCC method multiplies Project Construction Cost (PCC) by a group-specific fee rate. Classification determines which rate applies; PCC accuracy affects the resulting fee. The Architect's Guidelines distinguish between DAEDS (Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services — architect plus structural/MEP engineers) and DADS (Detailed Architectural Design Services — architecture only, approximately 60% of DAEDS). The 10 Project Classification Groups represent progressively complex building types.

### Worked Example 1: Group 1 Simple Warehouse

A warehouse project (Group 1: Simplest Utilization) has an estimated PCC of ₱30 million. Group 1 DAEDS fee for projects ≤₱50M is 5% of PCC.

Calculation: ₱30M × 5% = ₱1,500,000 total fee.

SPP 202 Phase distribution (SD=15%, DD=20%, CD=50%, Bidding=5%, CA=10%): Schematic Design ₱225,000 | Design Development ₱300,000 | Contract Documents ₱750,000 | Bidding Assistance ₱75,000 | Construction Administration ₱150,000.

### Worked Example 2: Group 2 Office with Sliding Scale

An office building (Group 2: Moderate Complexity) has PCC of ₱120M. Group 2 DAEDS applies a sliding scale: 6% for first ₱50M, 5% for next ₱50M, 4% for remaining amount.

Calculation: (₱50M × 6%) + (₱50M × 5%) + (₱20M × 4%) = ₱3M + ₱2.5M + ₱0.8M = ₱6.3M total fee.

Phase distribution: Schematic Design ₱945,000 | Design Development ₱1,260,000 | Contract Documents ₱3,150,000 | Bidding Assistance ₱315,000 | Construction Administration ₱630,000.

### Worked Example 3: Group 4 Single-Family Residence

A residential house (Group 4: Low-Rise Residential) has PCC of ₱8M. Group 4 DAEDS fee is flat 10% of PCC regardless of cost brackets.

Calculation: ₱8M × 10% = ₱800,000 total fee.

Phase distribution: Schematic Design ₱120,000 | Design Development ₱160,000 | Contract Documents ₱400,000 | Bidding Assistance ₱40,000 | Construction Administration ₱80,000.

### Worked Example 4: Group 9 Renovation at Enhanced Rate

A Group 2 office renovation (Group 9: Renovations) has PCC of ₱50M. Group 9 applies 150% multiplier to the base group's basic fee rate. Base Group 2 fee: ₱50M × 6% = ₱3M. Renovation enhancement: ₱3M × 150% = ₱4.5M total fee.

Phase distribution: Schematic Design ₱675,000 | Design Development ₱900,000 | Contract Documents ₱2,250,000 | Bidding Assistance ₱225,000 | Construction Administration ₱450,000.

### Worked Example 5: DAEDS vs DADS Comparison

Same ₱40M warehouse (Group 1), showing the difference between full DAEDS and architecture-only DADS. DAEDS (all disciplines): ₱40M × 5% = ₱2,000,000. DADS (architecture only, approximately 60% of DAEDS): ₱40M × 3% = ₱1,200,000. Difference: ₱800,000 (the engineering component).

When a client engages only an architect without structural or MEP consultants under separate contracts, DADS applies. When architects coordinate all disciplines, DAEDS applies.

## Key Provisions

| Group | Building Type | DAEDS Rate (≤₱50M) | Above ₱50M Scale |
|-------|---------------|--------------------|------------------|
| 1 | Warehouses, factories | 5% | 4%, 3%, 2%, 1%, 0.5% |
| 2 | Offices, schools | 6% | 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%, 1% |
| 3 | Churches, museums | 7% | 6%, 5%, 4%, 3%, 2% |
| 4 | Low-rise residential | 10% | Flat rate |
| 5 | Monumental buildings | 12% | Flat rate |
| 6 | Repetitive buildings | Varies by unit count | Declining percentages |
| 7 | Repetitive housing | 10% (1st) +60% (2-10) +30% (11+) | Modular reduction |
| 8 | Interior + site planning | 15% | Flat rate |
| 9 | Renovations | 150% of base group rate | Applied to basic fee |
| 10 | Technical consultation | MDPE method | No percentage |

DADS = approximately 60% of DAEDS rate (used when architect contracts separately from engineers). Phase percentages per SPP 202: Schematic Design 15%, Design Development 20%, Contract Documents 50%, Bidding Assistance 5%, Construction Administration 10%.

## Philippine Practice Context

In Philippine architectural practice, the Architect's Guidelines fee computation reflects the complexity and risk associated with different building types. Warehouses and factories (Group 1) require straightforward design; residential towers (Group 4-5) demand sophisticated systems coordination. Renovations (Group 9) incur premium fees due to hidden conditions and phasing constraints. Practitioners must verify PCC estimates before committing to fees; underestimated construction costs lead to unprofitable projects.

## How It's Tested

Exams test four competencies: (1) recognizing project group classification, (2) selecting correct fee percentage from the Architect's Guidelines, (3) computing total and phased fees accurately, and (4) distinguishing DAEDS from DADS and applying sliding scales correctly. Calculation accuracy is non-negotiable.

<Tip>
Memory aid: Groups 1-3 slide down (5→4→3→2→1; 6→5→4→3→2; 7→6→5→4→3). Groups 4-5 flat. Group 6-7 repeat diminishing. Group 8 premium. Group 9 multiplier (150%). Group 10 negotiated.
</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList>
- **Ignoring sliding scleas for Groups 1-3.** Always calculate each bracket separately: first ₱50M at base rate, next ₱50M at (base−1%), etc.
- **Confusing DAEDS and DADS percentages.** DADS is approximately 60% of DAEDS. If problem specifies "architect only," apply DADS.
- **Miscalculating phase payments.** SPP 202 percentages apply to total fee, not PCC. Total fee first, then distribute by phase.
- **Forgetting Group 9 is 150% of base, not 150% total.** If base Group 2 fee is ₱3M, Group 9 renovation = ₱3M × 1.5 = ₱4.5M.
- **Applying flat Group 4-5 rates when project exceeds ₱50M.** Groups 4 and 5 have no sliding sclea; 10% and 12% apply to entire PCC.
- **Not distinguishing renovation scope from new construction.** Group 9 applies only to renovation work, not new additions treated as separate projects.
</WikiMistakeList>

---

## Related Articles

- [Project Classification Groups](lea-prac-cmp-001)
- [Factors Determining Classification](lea-prac-cmp-002)
- [Project Construction Cost](lea-prac-cmp-003)
- [Schedule of Payments](lea-prac-cmp-004)
- [MDPE Formula](lea-prac-cmp-006)
- [MDPE Multipliers](lea-prac-cmp-007)
- [MDPE vs. Percentage of PCC](lea-prac-cmp-008)
- [Reimbursable Expenses](lea-prac-cmp-011)
- [SPP Doc 202 Phase Framework](lea-prac-svc-004)
- [Standard Owner-Architect Agreement](lea-prac-ctr-001)

rows.title: Spanish Colonial Architecture in Latin America
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal

Identify the three-part formula of Spanish colonial urban design in Latin America — Laws of the Indies grid plan, central plaza, cathedral — and explain how the Leyes de Indias (1573) imposed standardized city layouts across diverse geographies and cultures.
## Core Concept

Spanish colonialism imposed a distinctive architectural and urban order across Latin America from the 16th to 18th centuries. The **Laws of the Indies** (1573), issued by King Philip II, codified the design of every colonial town. Colonizers did not build randomly—they built according to rigid orthogonal grids that prioritized the plaza mayor (main square) as the civic and religious heart. This plaza anchored the cathedral, governor's palace, and municipal buildings in a hierarchical arrangement that reflected Spanish Crown authority.


<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-013-01-core-concept" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="View of the Plaza de Armas (Plaza Mayor) of Cusco, Peru, showing the central plaza with cathedral and cabildo, surrounded by colonial arcaded buildings on the grid plan established by the Laws of the Indies (1573)." caption="Plaza Mayor of Cusco — Spanish Colonial Grid Plan" suggestedAsset="Architectural reference image or diagram" placementIntent="Visual reference for architectural period/typology" />


<Tip>Memory aid: **"Laws = Grid + Plaza + Cathedral"** — the three-part formula that unified Spanish colonial urban design across the Americas from 1573 onward.</Tip>

Colonial architecture synthesized Spanish Baroque aesthetics with indigenous labor and local materials. Architects drew from late medieval Spanish traditions, mannerist ornamentation, and Baroque emotional intensity. However, indigenous craftspeople adapted Spanish forms to local stone, climate, and spiritual traditions, creating a hybrid aesthetic. Stone masonry, thick walls for thermal mass, and fortress-like designs (many churches doubled as defensive structures) became standard across Mexico, Peru, Colombia, and Central America.

<Note>Colonial architecture is not purely Spanish—it is a hybrid creation shaped by indigenous craftspeople, who adapted Spanish Baroque forms to local materials, climate, and pre-existing spatial traditions. This synthesis is called mestizo Baroque.</Note>

The **plaza mayor** itself functioned as a multipurpose space: market, assembly ground, bullfighting arena, and processional theater. Colonnades and portleas (covered arcades) surrounded the plaza, providing shade and defining public boundaries. The cathedral dominated one side, visually anchoring spiritual authority. This planning system produced coherence across colonial cities—Quito, Lima, Mexico City, Cartagena, and Havana all follow the same basic orthogonal logic, making the Laws of the Indies one of the first codified urban design systems in the Americas.

<Warn>Do not confuse the plaza mayor with indigenous gathering spaces, though they share a central function. The Laws of the Indies plaza is orthogonal, gridded, and explicitly hierarchical (cathedral + government buildings at fixed positions). Indigenous plazas were pre-contact but adapted into the colonial model—the plaza is syncretic, not purely European.</Warn>


<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-013-01-core-concept" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="Diagram showing the standardized Leyes de Indias city layout: central plaza (250 ft × 350 ft minimum), cardinal streets radiating from plaza corners, grid blocks for residents, and the siting of cathedral, government palace, and cabildo around the plaza." caption="Laws of the Indies — Standardized City Plan" suggestedAsset="Architectural reference image or diagram" placementIntent="Visual reference for architectural period/typology" />


## Key Facts and Testable Items

<WikiExamTable headers={["Element", "Purpose", "Characteristics"]} rows={[['["**Plaza Mayor**", "Civic and religious center", "Rectangular, surrounded by colonnades, cathedral on one side"]', '["**Laws of the Indies (1573)**", "Urban planning code", "Orthogonal grid, specific measurements for streets, plaza dimensions regulated"]', '["**Cathedral**", "Spiritual and civic authority", "Large façade, barrel vault or dome, mestizo baroque ornamentation"]', '["**Portleas (Colonnades)**", "Commercial and social space", "Covered arcades around plaza for shade and commerce"]', '["**Fortress Churches**", "Defense and worship", "Thick walls, minimal windows, gun ports in some examples"]', '["**Mestizo Baroque**", "Hybrid aesthetic", "Indigenous motifs integrated with Spanish Baroque ornamentation"]']]} />
## How It's Tested on the LEA

<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Urban Planning Recognition**
Questions ask you to identify the Laws of the Indies principles in a town plan diagram—orthogonal grid, plaza at center, cathedral dominance, radiating streets. You must name the planning system and explain why Spanish colonizers used it.</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Building Function and Form**
Questions present colonial churches or civic buildings and ask why they were designed a certain way—fortress-like walls (defense), thick masonry (climate control), multiple chapels (conversion of indigenous populations). You connect form to colonial function.</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Regional Variation**
Questions distinguish colonial architecture across regions: Mexican Baroque differs from Peruvian mestizo style differs from Caribbean island adaptations. You recognize local materials and indigenous influence while identifying shared Spanish colonial principles.</ExamTip>

<Callout>The LEA tests your understanding of **Spanish Colonial** urban planning principles, the **Laws of the Indies**, and the architectural characteristics of colonial churches and civic spaces across Latin America. This knowledge appears in both history and theory questions about colonial planning grids and Baroque ecclesiastical design.</Callout>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing colonial dates" correction="Students say \"colonial period\" without specifying region or time. Spanish colonialism began 1492 in the Caribbean, 1519 in Mexico, 1532 in Peru. The Laws of the Indies apply from 1573 onward, not to all colonial building." context="Date your answers: \"mid-16th-century Peru,\" \"early-17th-century Mexico.\"" />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Forgetting indigenous contribution" correction="Students attribute entire colonial architecture to Spain. Indigenous craftspeople and communities shaped every building—they quarried stone, designed decorative programs influenced by pre-Columbian motifs, and adapted Spanish forms to local climate and labor practices." context="Say \"mestizo\" or \"hybrid\" explicitly." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating plaza mayor as purely European. The plaza is not a straight Spanish import. Indigenous communities had central gathering spaces; colonizers adapted this tradition into the Laws of the Indies orthogonal model. Colonial architecture is fusion, not replacement.", "Ignoring defensive architecture. Many colonial churches are fortress-like because they were fortresses. Students overlook gun ports, minimal windows, and thick walls as defensive features. A church with a gun port is not a design accident—it reflects 16th-century colonial military reality."]} />

## Key Terms

**Laws of the Indies** — Code of urban planning and building standards issued 1573 by King Philip II; mandated orthogonal grids, plaza dimensions, and hierarchical civic arrangement across Spanish colonies.

**Plaza Mayor** — Central rectangular plaza in colonial town; anchored by cathedral and government buildings; functioned as market, assembly, and processional space.

**Mestizo Baroque** — Hybrid style combining Spanish Baroque ornament with indigenous decorative and spiritual traditions; created by indigenous craftspeople working under Spanish architectural direction.

**Portleas** — Covered colonnades surrounding colonial plazas; provided shade and defined public commercial space.

**Orthogonal Grid** — Rectilinear street pattern at right angles; the basis of Laws of the Indies urban planning.

**Barrel Vault** — Continuous semicircular roof spanning a rectangular space; common in colonial churches for large interior spans without columns.

**Mestizaje** — Cultural and artistic blending of Spanish and indigenous traditions; visible in colonial architecture through decoration, materials, and spatial adaptation.

**Fortress Church** — Religious building designed with defensive features—thick walls, gun ports, minimal windows—reflecting 16th-17th-century colonial security needs.

<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-013-01-core-concept-timeline" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="Plan diagram of a Spanish colonial city according to the Laws of Indias (1573): orthogonal grid plan with central plaza mayor anchoring the cathedral, governor's palace, and municipal buildings, showing standardized colonial urban design." caption="Spanish Colonial — Laws of the Indies Grid Plan" suggestedAsset="Timeline diagram" placementIntent="Timeline diagram for architectural period" />

## Related Articles

See also within Latin American Architecture: **lea-hist-013-02-core-concept**.
